title: India's Tax Revolution Enters Year 10 — and the Next Phase Is Being Built by Machines
excerpt: GST 2.0 is shifting from digitisation to AI-driven enforcement, database integration and a two-tier rate structure that has already lifted business confidence to near-universal levels
body:
When President Pranab Mukherjee stood in the central hall of the old Parliament building at the stroke of midnight on July 1, 2017, and inaugurated the Goods and Services Tax, the mood was part ceremony, part gamble. Prime Minister Narendra Modi called it a "good and simple tax." Industry called it a headache. Small businesses called it worse.

Nine years later, the gamble has paid off — and the next phase is barely recognisable from the reform that launched.

## The Numbers Tell the Story

The scale of transformation is hard to overstate. GST replaced 17 central and state taxes and 13 cesses with a single indirect tax framework — the most sweeping fiscal reform since independence. The registered taxpayer base has more than doubled, from 66.5 lakh at launch to roughly 1.6 crore in 2026. Average monthly collections have risen from ₹89,700 crore in its first year to ₹1.85 lakh crore in FY26, with annual gross revenue hitting ₹22.27 lakh crore — an 8.3 per cent jump over the previous year.

A Deloitte survey released this week found that more than 99 per cent of businesses now report a positive or neutral experience with GST. Negative sentiment has dropped to near zero, down from 10 per cent in 2022 and 5 per cent in 2025. For a reform that once triggered street protests and a compliance crisis, that is a remarkable turnaround.

## GST 2.0 — From Digitisation to Intelligence

The bigger shift is what comes next. GST 2.0, formally launched in September 2025, moved the system from multiple rate slabs — 5, 12, 18, and 28 per cent — to a streamlined two-tier framework: 5 per cent and 18 per cent for most goods and services, with a 40 per cent slab retained only for luxury and so-called sin goods like sugary drinks.

Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman has described the overhaul as a deliberate strategy to "leave more cash with taxpayers" while tightening enforcement through technology rather than inspectors. The government plans to integrate GST, income tax, and customs databases into a single risk-assessment framework — using artificial intelligence to flag evasion, cross-verify transactions, and reduce manual intervention, particularly for micro, small, and medium enterprises.

For MSMEs, the quarterly return filing scheme has seen a sharp uptick in acceptance, with positive responses rising from 12 per cent in 2023 to 67 per cent in 2026. E-invoicing and e-way bill systems, once sources of confusion, are now cited by 48 per cent of businesses as key drivers of improved compliance.

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRIs running businesses in India — and there are more of them every year — the unified tax regime has quietly eliminated one of the biggest headaches: navigating a patchwork of state-level taxes that once required separate registrations, separate filings, and separate headaches for every state a company operated in.

Cross-border e-invoicing, streamlined refund processing, and AI-driven compliance checks mean that an NRI entrepreneur managing an MSME from Houston or London faces considerably less paperwork than five years ago. The formalisation of the economy — 1.6 crore registered taxpayers, up from 66.5 lakh — also means a more transparent business environment for diaspora investors channelling capital back into India.

The shift matters for remittances too. A formalised economy with robust tax compliance translates into better credit ratings, lower borrowing costs, and ultimately stronger returns on the investments that NRIs are making in Indian real estate, startups, and mutual funds.

## The Unfinished Business

Not everything has been resolved. Petroleum products — crude oil, petrol, diesel, ATF, and natural gas — remain outside the GST framework, a concession to states that depend heavily on fuel taxes for revenue. The GST Council has discussed bringing aviation turbine fuel under the regime, but the proposal has not found favour with state governments.

Rate rationalisation continues to be debated. Consumer goods and life sciences have seen the strongest impact from rate cuts, but some sectors still argue that the structure is too complex for their specific supply chains.

And then there is the question of whether AI enforcement will be a tool for efficiency or a new source of friction. Automated flags and cross-database verification sound efficient in a policy paper. In practice, they will need to distinguish between genuine evasion and the messy reality of small-business bookkeeping.

## What Comes Next

The direction is clear: fewer rates, smarter enforcement, and deeper digital integration. Empirical studies suggest that a 1 per cent growth in GST revenue has led to a 0.56 per cent increase in GDP — a correlation that gives the government strong reason to keep pushing.

As GST enters its tenth year, the question is no longer whether the reform was worth the disruption. It is whether the machines now being trained on India's tax data can make the system as good as its architects always claimed it would be.
